newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Control of Hebron test for PLO security chief.
newsitem.headline: Control of Hebron test for PLO security chief.

text.p: Yasser Arafat's security chief in Hebron stood deep in recollection on Thursday in a small cell where he said Israeli jailers tortured him.
Jibril Rajoub, head of the plainclothes Palestinian Preventive Security service, now makes his headquarters in the building in which he had been held prisoner.

"I was a fighter against Israeli occupation. In 1985 I spent 35 days in this cell which is only two square metres. Here they tortured me and beat me so I went on a hunger strike for 33 days," Rajoub told Reuters.

Rajoub, 44, heads the strongest Palestinan security apparatus in the West Bank. An active member of Palestinian President Arafat's mainstream Fatah faction, he was jailed by Israel for 17 years and then deported to south Lebanon in 1987.

Rajoub returned as security commander in Arafat's Palestinian Authority in 1994 following the signing of the landmark 1993 PLO-Israel peace deal which gave Palestinians self-rule in parts of the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
"All the time I was in prison I was sure that one day I will be free and that one day we will be the governors of this area because we are the legal owners here," Rajoub said.
Although Arafat has formed over eight different security agencies in the West Bank, Rajoub has stood out as a "strongman" both feared and respected by Palestinians.
His men, all Fatah members who were active during the seven-year Palestinian uprising against Israeli occupation, operate in all parts of the West Bank.
But Rajoub's real test is in Hebron, a flashpoint of violence between Jews and Moslems and a stronghold of the militant Islamic Resistance Movement Hamas.

He moved his headquarters from Jericho to Hebron last week immediately after Israel's handover of most of the city to the PLO. One-fifth of Hebron remains under Israeli control to protect some 400 Jews who have settled among 30,000 Palestinians in its centre.

"President Arafat instructed me to move to Hebron because Hebron is a special case and therefore it needs special commanders," Rajoub said. "I'm sure I will succeed in controlling the area. I have never known failure."

In the city where family ties are very strong, Hebron's more than 100,000 Palestinians respect Rajoub and have already shown him they were willing to cooperate. But he made it clear he would not allow his people to violate the law or the PLO-Israel peace deals.
"If someone under our jurisdiction tries to create a problem, we will deal with them and we know how," he said.

Rajoub said he did not believe Palestinians would initiate trouble in Hebron and that he was sure Hamas and other rejectionist factions would respect the PLO's commitments to Israel and oppose the accords peacefully.

"I'm worried about those who have an interest to destroy, to kill the process and I think the only party that has the interest to stop the process are the settlers who want to prevent redeployments from the West Bank," he said.

Calling all Jewish settlements in the West Bank and Gaza illegal, Rajoub lashed out at those who regard Baruch Goldstein, a U.S.-born settler who massacred 29 Arab worshippers in a Hebron mosque in 1994.
"Those who created Goldstein...danced on his grave and dealt with him as a hero, we don't want them and they don't have a place among us here," he said.
